---
title: "Hurricane Michael: Wind Speed vs. Wave Height"
---

```{R}
#| echo: false
#| message: false
#| warning: false
devtools::load_all()
library(tidyverse)
```

NOAA's National Data Buoy Center operates moored buoy **42039**, in the eastern Gulf of Mexico (28.97N, 86.01W), reporting hourly standard meteorological observations. We use two channels:

- `WSPD`: wind speed (m/s), 8-minute average
- `WVHT`: significant wave height (m), average of the highest one-third of waves in a 20-minute sampling window

**Hurricane Michael** formed in the southwestern Caribbean on 2018-10-07, became a hurricane at 2018-10-08 00:00 UTC, and rapidly intensified into a Category 5 system before making landfall near Mexico Beach, Florida on 2018-10-10. Buoy 42039 sat close enough to the track to record the approach in real time — and stopped transmitting at 2018-10-10 08:50 UTC, with pressure down to 985.8 hPa and wind speed up to 24.0 m/s, as the storm's core closed in. We treat 2018-10-08 00:00 UTC (when Michael became a hurricane) through the last observation as the storm regime, and the five preceding weeks (2018-09-01 onward) as baseline.

Wind speed and wave height are mechanistically linked — local wind stress is what builds a sea state — so some correlation is expected in any weather regime. The interesting question is whether a storm of this intensity changes that relationship, or just scales it up.

```{R buoy-load}
#| echo: false
#| message: false
#| label: buoy-load

X_raw <- read_table(
  "../data/real-data/hurricane-michael-buoy/42039h2018_raw.txt",
  comment = "#",
  col_names = c("YY", "MM", "DD", "hh", "mm", "WDIR", "WSPD", "GST", "WVHT",
                "DPD", "APD", "MWD", "PRES", "ATMP", "WTMP", "DEWP", "VIS", "TIDE"),
  na = c("99", "99.0", "999", "9999.0", "99.00", "MM"),
  show_col_types = FALSE
) |>
  mutate(across(c(YY, MM, DD, hh, mm), as.integer)) |>
  mutate(datetime = as.POSIXct(sprintf("%04d-%02d-%02d %02d:%02d:00", YY, MM, DD, hh, mm), tz = "UTC"))

X_data <- X_raw |>
  filter(datetime >= as.POSIXct("2018-09-01 00:00", tz = "UTC"),
         datetime <= as.POSIXct("2018-10-10 08:50", tz = "UTC")) |>
  filter(!is.na(WSPD), !is.na(WVHT)) |>
  mutate(storm = datetime >= as.POSIXct("2018-10-08 00:00", tz = "UTC"))

X_mat <- as.matrix(X_data[, c("WSPD", "WVHT")])
colnames(X_mat) <- c("WindSpeed", "WaveHeight")
win <- 12
```

`r nrow(X_data)` hourly observations, 2018-09-01 through 2018-10-10 08:50 UTC (the buoy's last transmission), of which `r sum(X_data$storm)` fall in the storm window.

```{R buoy-oracle}
#| echo: false
#| label: buoy-oracle

oracle_resid <- function(X, grp) {
  R <- sapply(colnames(X), function(cn) X[, cn] - ave(X[, cn], grp))
  colnames(R) <- colnames(X)
  R
}

X_oracle <- oracle_resid(X_mat, X_data$storm)
```

```{R buoy-tables}
#| echo: false
#| label: buoy-tables

L_ece <- 150

ece_cor <- ece.cor(X_mat, L = L_ece) |> round(3)
rownames(ece_cor) <- colnames(ece_cor) <- colnames(X_mat)

oracle_cor  <- cor(X_oracle) |> round(3)
pearson_cor <- cor(X_mat) |> round(3)

ece_pmat     <- ece_pval(X_mat) |> round(3)
oracle_pmat  <- cor_pval(X_oracle) |> round(3)
pearson_pmat <- cor_pval(X_mat) |> round(3)

# ece.test()'s z-test hardcodes its internal block length (L = 2), which sits
# in this series' unstable small-L region -- compute the z-test by hand at
# the same L_ece used for the point estimate above.
ece_se_Lece  <- ece.cor.se(X_mat[, "WindSpeed"], X_mat[, "WaveHeight"], L = L_ece, kappa = "gaussian")
ece_z_pval   <- 2 * pnorm(abs(ece_cor[1, 2] / ece_se_Lece), lower.tail = FALSE)
```

::: {.panel-tabset}

## Plot

```{R fig-buoy-series}
#| echo: false
#| fig-cap: "Wind speed and significant wave height, buoy 42039, 2018-09-01 through the buoy's last transmission on 2018-10-10. Teal = storm regime (Michael a hurricane or stronger)."
#| fig-height: 6

X_data |>
  select(datetime, storm, WindSpeed = WSPD, WaveHeight = WVHT) |>
  pivot_longer(c(WindSpeed, WaveHeight), names_to = "series", values_to = "value") |>
  ggplot(aes(datetime, value, color = storm)) +
  geom_line(color = "gray70", linewidth = 0.2) +
  geom_point(size = 0.4) +
  facet_wrap(~series, ncol = 1, scales = "free_y") +
  labs(title = "Buoy 42039: Wind Speed and Wave Height, Hurricane Michael Approach", x = NULL, y = NULL, color = "Storm") +
  theme_minimal()
```

Both series climb together as Michael approaches, but the record ends mid-ramp — the buoy went dark at 08:50 UTC on 2018-10-10, roughly 33 hours before landfall, still recording rising wind and seas.

## ACF

::: {.panel-tabset}

### Oracle

```{R acf-buoy-oracle}
#| echo: false

par(mfrow = c(1, 2), mar = c(2, 3, 2, 1), oma = c(2, 0, 0, 0), mgp = c(1.8, 1, 0))
acf(X_oracle[, "WindSpeed"], main = "Wind Speed")
acf(X_oracle[, "WaveHeight"], main = "Wave Height")
mtext("Lag (hours)", side = 1, outer = TRUE, line = 0.5)
```

Lag-1 autocorrelation of roughly 0.91-0.94 survives storm-mean removal — sea state and wind both have real hour-to-hour momentum, more persistent than any other sensor chapter in this book (Detroit Lake's algal pigments sit around 0.72-0.73 by comparison).

### Oracle

```{R trend-buoy-oracle}

S_oracle <- X_oracle[, "WindSpeed"] * X_oracle[, "WaveHeight"]
S_smooth <- stats::filter(S_oracle, rep(1 / win, win), sides = 2)

par(mar = c(3, 3, 1, 1), mgp = c(1.8, 1, 0))
ylim <- quantile(S_oracle, probs = c(0.01, 0.99), na.rm = TRUE)
```

## Correlation

```{R}
#| layout-ncol: 3
#| echo: false

knitr::kable(ece_cor,     caption = "ECE Correlation")
knitr::kable(oracle_cor,  caption = "Oracle Correlation")
knitr::kable(pearson_cor, caption = "Pearson Correlation")
```

Naive Pearson (0.888) and Oracle (0.823) agree that wind and waves are already tightly coupled — this is the Gulf of Mexico, not the open ocean, so local wind seas dominate even outside the storm (mean dominant wave period stays under 6 seconds at baseline, consistent with locally wind-driven chop rather than distant swell). Splitting by regime directly, Pearson correlation is 0.855 at baseline and 0.923 during the storm approach: real, but a modest tightening next to the roughly 4x jump in both series' means (wind 4.8 to 13.0 m/s, waves 0.73 to 3.74 m).

ECE at the usual block lengths (`L` = 2-50) is unstable and badly understates the relationship (0.21-0.47) — the near-unity autocorrelation above means a short block difference doesn't fully cancel each series' own momentum before correlating the two. Pushing `L` out to 125-200 (`L_ece` = `r L_ece` used above) recovers a real plateau around 0.72-0.73, in the same neighborhood as Oracle and Pearson but still visibly short of them. This series needs an order of magnitude more smoothing than Detroit Lake's `L = 50` to converge — a direct consequence of its much higher persistence, not a sign of a wrong point estimate.

## P-Values

```{R}
#| layout-ncol: 3
#| echo: false

knitr::kable(ece_pmat,     caption = "ECE P-Values (package default, L = 2)")
knitr::kable(oracle_pmat,  caption = "Oracle P-Values")
knitr::kable(pearson_pmat, caption = "Pearson P-Values")
```

Naive and Oracle both reject independence outright (p < 0.001). `ece_pval()` — which, like `ece.test(type = "z.test")`, hardcodes its internal block length to the package default `L = 2` — actually does reject here too (p = `r ece_pmat[1,2]`), but that's testing the badly biased `L = 2` point estimate (0.208, from the Correlation tab's sweep), not the `L_ece` = `r L_ece` estimate the plateau above settled on. Computing the z-test by hand at `L_ece` instead (`ece.cor.se(..., L = L_ece)`) gives se = `r round(ece_se_Lece, 4)`, p = `r format(ece_z_pval, scientific = TRUE, digits = 3)` — a decisive rejection, this time backed by the converged point estimate rather than the unstable one. Both land on "reject," but for different, and not equally trustworthy, reasons.

:::

---

## Bootstrap Methods

```{R}
#| echo: false
ece.test(X_mat, type = "bs.multiplier")
ece.test(X_mat, type = "bs.parametric")
```

Both bootstrap variants use a fixed lag-1 difference internally (independent of `L_ece`), so they inherit the small-block instability rather than the large-`L` plateau. Across repeated runs, the multiplier bootstrap gives p ≈ 0.08-0.12 — hovering right at the α = 0.10 boundary, sometimes rejecting, sometimes not — while the parametric bootstrap gives p ≈ 0.58-0.61, clearly failing to reject. Neither is as decisive as the hand-computed `L_ece` z-test above.

## Where this leaves us

Hurricane Michael gives ECE a real, sharply dated mechanism — the buoy's own last transmission marks the moment the storm made the observation impossible — and a textbook mechanistically-linked pair (wind stress builds a sea state). Unlike the mean-shift chapters elsewhere in this book, the correlation itself barely moves (0.855 to 0.923): the storm's signature here is almost entirely a change in scale, wind and waves both roughly quadrupling, with the underlying coupling staying strong throughout.

That scale change is exactly what ECE is built to see past, and at large enough `L` it does — the estimate converges to 0.72-0.73, in the right neighborhood as Oracle (0.823) and Pearson (0.888). But it needs `L` in the hundreds to get there, far past what any other chapter in this book requires, because this series' hour-to-hour persistence (lag-1 autocorrelation above 0.9) is the strongest of any sensor data used so far.

Inference tells a more tangled story than the point estimate does. The package's default z-test (`L = 2`) rejects independence, but off a point estimate (0.208) the Correlation tab already showed is badly biased — the right answer for the wrong reason. Hand-computing the z-test at the converged `L_ece` rejects too, this time credibly. The two bootstrap methods, built on a fixed lag-1 difference neither exposes for adjustment, land closer to the `L = 2` regime than the plateau — one borderline, one a clear non-rejection. Four tests, three different levels of trustworthiness, all nominally answering the same question. The result is a clean illustration of a tradeoff that's easy to state and easy to miss: block-differencing needs `L` large relative to the autocorrelation's decay time, not just larger than some fixed default, and a persistent enough series can make the "obvious" choice of `L` — including the one built into the package's own hardcoded test — badly wrong without any diagnostic screaming about it until you check.
